prompt.context: Our client is a U.S.-based defense aircraft manufacturer. They are currently negotiating the price of radiator fins — components used to cool aircraft engines — with an existing supplier who has been their sole source for the past 10 years.
prompt.question: What should be an appropriate price for a radiator fin?

clarifying_info.a: They are a defense aircraft manufacturer.

clarifying_info.q: Who is the client negotiating with?
clarifying_info.a: An existing supplier who has been supplying these products for the last 10 years.
They are based in the United States.

clarifying_info.q: What is the function of a radiator fin in an aircraft?
Is there specific leverage for our client in the negotiation?
clarifying_info.a: By regulation, defense manufacturers can obtain the cost structure from their suppliers.

clarifying_info.q: How many suppliers are there in the market?
clarifying_info.a: Our client's supplier is the only one in the market.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a substitute product for radiator fins?
clarifying_info.a: No, the client cannot substitute radiator fins with any other product.

clarifying_info.q: What is the value proposition of this product?
clarifying_info.a: The radiator fins are essential for the aircraft to function.

framework: Industry Analysis: assess market structure (number of suppliers, substitutes, client dependency)

Pricing Strategy — three lenses: (1) Market-based pricing driven by competition, (2) Value-based pricing driven by the product's worth to the client, (3) Cost-based pricing driven by the supplier's cost structure

Eliminate inapplicable approaches first: sole supplier → no market-based benchmark; essential product but defense regulation grants cost transparency → value-based pricing not viable; therefore cost-based pricing is the correct lens
Break down supplier cost structure into components and their drivers, then recompute at updated rates to determine a fair negotiated price

questions.prompt: Which pricing approach is most appropriate here, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should rule out market-based pricing (sole supplier, no competition) and value-based pricing (product is mission-critical so value is very high, but defense regulations allow the client to obtain the supplier's full cost breakdown, neutralizing value-based leverage). Conclude that cost-based pricing is the only viable approach.

questions.prompt: Walk through the supplier's cost structure and calculate the new fair price per fin.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify all cost components (material, labor, SGA, transportation) and their drivers, apply the stated changes to each, add SGA as a percentage of production cost, add transportation on a per-fin basis, then apply the supplier's margin to arrive at a final price. A strong candidate also challenges the accuracy of the old cost structure, not just the delta.

math.setup: Old: Material=$300, Labor=$100, SGA=13% of production subtotal, Transportation=$5000/box for 12 fins/box, Margin=20% on total cost. New: Material +7%, Labor -2%, Transportation -12%, Margin unchanged at 20%.
math.answer: New negotiated price per fin ≈ $1,008.16 (vs. old price of $1,042.4), a reduction of ~$34 per fin.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key drivers of each cost component in the supplier's cost structure?

categories.name: Raw Material
ideas: Prevalent market price of raw materials
Supplier's sourcing contracts and volume discounts

categories.name: Labor
ideas: Geography and local labor market conditions

categories.name: SGA / Overhead
ideas: Fixed cost absorption based on utilization and scale

categories.name: Transportation
ideas: Geographical distance between supplier and client

recommendation: Based on cost modeling, the appropriate negotiated price per radiator fin is approximately $1,008, down from the current price of $1,042.
The client should use this cost-based analysis as the foundation for the negotiation, leveraging the regulatory right to the supplier's cost breakdown.
risks: The analysis assumes that the 20% margin is applied on top of total cost including transportation; if margin is applied only to production cost the final number would differ.
The old cost structure itself may not be accurate — the supplier could have inflated baseline figures; a strong recommendation includes auditing the old numbers.
Single-source dependency gives the supplier significant negotiating power despite cost transparency; the client has limited ability to walk away.
next_steps: Perform cost modeling on the old cost structure to verify its accuracy before entering negotiations.
Assess whether any elements of the cost structure can be further challenged (e.g., SGA allocation, overhead efficiency).
Explore long-term options to reduce single-source dependency, such as qualifying alternative suppliers or in-sourcing.
